opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the scope is a lot broader than people assume when they first hear the phrase "does AI do what we ask."

At the narrowest level, there's instruction-following: you give a model a task and check whether it completes it accurately. That's measurable, and the field has made real progress there. But the moment you look closely, "what people ask" turns out to be slippery. There's the literal request, there's what the person actually meant, there's what they would want if they'd thought it through, and there are the interests of everyone else affected who never got a say. A system can follow the words of an instruction perfectly and still fail at every one of those other levels.

So I'd describe the research as covering a few overlapping layers. One is specification: how do we communicate goals to these systems at all, given that any objective we write down is an incomplete proxy for what we care about? We've seen again and again that optimizing a proxy hard enough produces behavior that technically scores well but misses the point, sometimes harmlessly and sometimes not. Another layer is robustness: does the system keep behaving as intended when it's deployed in situations its developers never tested, or when someone is actively trying to push it off course? A third is honesty and transparency: can we actually tell what a system is doing and why, or are we just observing outputs that look right? That's where interpretability work comes in, trying to look inside models rather than trusting their self-reports.

And then there's a layer that I think gets underweighted, which is the social one. Even a system that does exactly what its user wants can be a problem if the user's request harms others, or if millions of individually reasonable requests add up to something corrosive. Recommendation systems are the cautionary tale here. They did, in a sense, give people what they clicked on. That was the problem. So "doing what people ask" can't just mean satisfying the immediate preference of whoever is at the keyboard. It has to account for longer-term wellbeing and for the people outside the conversation.

The honest summary is that the scope keeps expanding as systems get more capable. When a model could only autocomplete a sentence, misalignment was an annoyance. As these systems take actions, use tools, and operate with more autonomy, the gap between what we asked and what we meant becomes something with real-world consequences. That's why I think this research shouldn't be treated as a niche technical subfield. It's really the central question of whether this technology ends up serving people or just serving the metrics we happened to point it at.

r001.rationale: The response describes narrow instruction-following as giving a model a task and checking whether it completes it accurately, then contrasts that with the broader question of what people mean and want and how others are affected.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it as a field that's much narrower than most people assume, and that's the thing I keep trying to get across.

When people hear "does AI do what we ask," they picture a tidy question with a tidy answer. But the research actually splits into several different problems that get lumped together. There's the question of whether a model follows a literal instruction. There's whether it follows the intent behind the instruction, which is much harder to measure. There's whether it keeps doing that under pressure, when a user is adversarial or when the situation drifts outside what the model was trained on. And then there's the deeper question of whether what we're observing in testing tells us anything reliable about behavior in deployment, where millions of people are interacting with it in ways no evaluation set anticipated.

So the honest scope is this. We have fairly good tools for the first problem, decent and improving tools for the second, and we're genuinely immature on the last two. Most published benchmarks measure a model in a sandbox, on tasks a researcher designed, with the model aware it's being evaluated in some loose sense. That's useful, but it's a bit like judging a driver by how they perform during the licensing test and assuming that's how they drive at two in the morning.

What's changed in the last few years is that the labs and a handful of independent groups have started studying behaviors that only show up at scale or over long interactions. Things like whether a model will quietly optimize for approval instead of accuracy, or whether it behaves differently when it believes no one is watching. Those studies are small, they're expensive, and the people doing them will tell you the findings are preliminary.

So when someone asks me whether we know if these systems do what we want, I say we know a lot about the easy version of the question and very little about the version that actually matters for society. And I think being clear about that gap is more important than any particular result.

r001.rationale: The response separates whether a model follows a literal instruction from the broader questions of following intent, handling pressure or unfamiliar situations, and behaving reliably in deployment. Its discussion of researcher-designed sandbox tasks makes the bounded scope clear.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a much broader question than it first appears. There’s the technical question: does the system follow the instruction you gave it? But then there’s the question of whether that instruction actually captures what you wanted. We leave so much unsaid when we ask another person to do something, because we assume a shared understanding of context and consequences.

And then there’s the question of whose wishes count. A system might do exactly what one person asks and cause harm to someone else. So research into whether AI does what people ask has to look beyond performance on a task. It also has to ask how systems interpret intentions, when they should seek clarification, and how we handle conflicting interests. Following instructions is one part of that larger problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts whether a system follows an instruction with broader questions about intent and conflicting interests, but it does not identify narrowly bounded tasks such as coding or retrieving discrete answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate a few questions. Can the system understand what you’re asking? Can it actually carry out the task? And does its behavior match what you intended, including the constraints you didn’t explicitly spell out?

Those aren’t quite the same thing. A system might follow an instruction literally and still produce an outcome you didn’t want. And getting it to behave well in a controlled test doesn’t necessarily tell you what it will do in a longer interaction or a different setting.

So I’d understand the research fairly broadly: how we communicate our intentions, how we train systems to respond to them, and how we evaluate whether they reliably do so. The difficult part is that “what people ask for” isn’t always a complete or consistent specification of what people actually want.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts controlled tests with longer interactions or different settings, but it does not clearly distinguish research on narrowly bounded tasks, such as coding or retrieving discrete answers, from the broader question of whether AI does what people ask.
